title: The chain back to him
hookLine: every Muslim alive learned from someone, back to the companions
tomorrow: Year three close: the long story

cards: Who taught you to tie your shoes? The name may be gone already. Try another: who taught you the first prayer you knew, or the first verse, or the first words of a language you love?
Sometimes that name comes back. Now ask who taught them, and who taught that person. For the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ, Muslims say the thread doesn't vanish into fog.
It runs back, teacher before teacher, to the companions who heard him. Each person along it is one link.

teach.b: First, the word. Open a hadith collection and the reports begin with names: so-and-so told us that so-and-so told him, that so-and-so heard the Prophet say. That list of names is the isnad, the chain a saying leans on.
Scholars weighed each link: was this person honest, careful, did they actually meet the one they quote? Second, why it mattered.
In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak is quoted saying, in effect, that the isnad is part of the religion, and without it anyone could say whatever they liked.
The chain was a guard against invention. Third, the chain is people, not paper.

teach.h: IJAZA: A LIST OF TEACHERS IN YOUR HAND.
teach.b: Qur'an recitation is still taught face to face, the student reading to a teacher who listens and corrects, and some receive a written permission, an ijaza, that lists their teachers, and their teachers' teachers.

teach.h: CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: The Prophet said, in Sahih al-Bukhari: convey from me, even a single verse.

teach.h: LEARN THE QUR'AN AND TEACH IT.
teach.b: And in another hadith there: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. Learning is only half of it. The isnad itself names particular transmitters, weighed one by one.

But the command to convey asks for as little as one verse, and the same habit of passing on runs through lives no chain records: a mother teaching a du'a, a neighbor showing a new Muslim how to make wudu, a teacher who stayed late.
Everything this year has told was carried this way. Not by a book alone, but by a chain of people.

how: Hadith are studied with their chains of narrators, and Qur'an recitation is traditionally learned face to face with a teacher; some receive an ijaza, a permission to teach that names the teachers before them.

games.q: you are an early scholar. someone brings you a saying they say comes from the Prophet. what do you ask first?
o: who told you, and who told them?
games.why: scholars asked for the chain and weighed each link. without the isnad, as Ibn al-Mubarak warned, anyone could say whatever they liked.

practice: Pick one thing you know by heart, a verse, a du'a, a recipe, a line of advice, and say it to yourself once, slowly.
Then ask whose voice you first heard it in: that person is your link, and if you can, go one step further back to where they got it.
If you pray, you can make du'a for that teacher, living or gone; if not, simply hold a quiet thank-you for them.

wordCard.voice: Isnad, the chain of narrators a hadith leans on, teacher before teacher, back to the companions who heard the Prophet himself. Today's word.
